name: The Night Watchman
role: The office's security: how it stands, and what is different from normal
greet.4: Hear, you people, and let me tell you …
fit.yes: Every server can use a watch at night. His first round notes what is normal.
fire_note: Nothing keeps running: his rounds stop. His watch book stays — hired again, he takes a fresh look at what is normal.
bubble.first: My first round is still to come. Then I note what is normal.

bubble.open.one: One entry you don't know yet.

round_now_title: Walk a round right away instead of waiting for the next one
round_failed: The round went wrong — the messenger's log says why.
notify_off: No more reports to Unraid's notifications. All of it stays in the watch book.
notify_missing: Unraid's notification script isn't there — I can't report anything.
round.title: The last round
round.sub: Every five minutes, also with the office closed. He only reads what lives in RAM or on the flash — no disk wakes up.
round.first: His first round records what is normal now — nothing is reported for it.
round.failed: The last round went wrong — the messenger's log says why. He tries again at the next one.
round.skipped: The syslog grew by more than {size} since the round before — he read the newest part only.
round.no_docker: Docker didn't answer on the last round — containers were left out.
round.no_shares: Unraid's list of shares wasn't there on the last round — shares were left out.
posture.title: How secure does it stand?
posture.sub: How it stands now — not what changed. What I would set differently, and why. Advice, no alarm: nothing goes to Unraid's notifications or into the watch book; the team lead only hears how many. «I know, thanks» puts a tip aside for every browser, until what it is about changes.
posture.none: Nothing to say. It stands well.
posture.show_again_title: Count it again: in my bubble and at the team lead
posture.ack_title: Put it aside for every browser — it comes back when what it is about changes
posture.level_info_text: Can be right as it is — as long as you know.

posture.public.title.one: Open to everyone in the network: {names}
posture.public.title.other: {n} shares open to everyone in the network: {names}

posture.public.why: Security «Public»: anyone in your network may read, write and delete there — every device, every guest, every infected laptop. Set it to «Secure» (everyone reads, chosen users write) or «Private», and give your users access. A disk, a pool or the flash counts too.
posture.telnet.title: Telnet is on
posture.telnet.why: Telnet sends everything unencrypted, the root password too. SSH does the same, encrypted. Switch Telnet off under Management Access.
posture.ftp.title: Unraid's FTP server is on
posture.ftp.why: FTP sends passwords and files unencrypted. If you don't need it, switch it off; for files over the network SMB or SFTP (comes with SSH) are the better choice.
posture.mitigations_off.title: CPU protection switched off (mitigations=off)
posture.mitigations_off.why: Your {cpu} boots without the protections against Spectre-like flaws; open now: {open}. That gives a few percent of speed (much more on older Intel, less on newer CPUs and AMD). Off is fine when only you and programs you trust run here. On is better as soon as VMs or containers run code you don't control, others use the server, or services are reachable from the internet. AMD is affected too — by its own flaws (e.g. SRSO, Retbleed, TSA). To switch on: remove «mitigations=off» under Settings → Boot Parameters, then reboot.

posture.vmscape.title.one: VMScape: a VM could read the host
posture.vmscape.title.other: VMScape: {n} VMs could read the host

posture.vmscape.why: This 2025 flaw lets a guest read memory of the host's VM process (QEMU) — exactly what the switched-off protection would cover. With VMs only you use it matters little; with VMs others use, or that run untrusted software, switch the protection back on.
posture.privileged.why: A privileged container may do nearly anything on the server — fine for tools that need it (hardware, VPN, the backup), worth a second look for everything else. On the Docker page: Edit → Privileged off, and see whether it still works. A container that turns privileged later goes into my watch book.
posture.mitigations_on.title: CPU protection is on
posture.mitigations_on.why: Your {cpu} runs with the protections against Spectre-like flaws — the safe default. It costs a few percent of speed, more on older Intel CPUs. Switching it off only pays when nothing here runs code you don't trust and nothing is reachable from the internet.
book.title: Watch book
book.sub: What was different from normal, newest first. «I know, thanks» makes that state the new normal — then only what changes after it is told again.
ack_title: Make this the new normal: it leaves what's open and isn't told again.
ack_all_title: Everything open in the watch book becomes the new normal

ack_all_text.one: One entry becomes the new normal: what it names (an address, rights, a plugin, a file, a share). Only what changes after that is told again.
ack_all_text.other: {n} entries become the new normal: what they name (addresses, rights, plugins, files, shares). Only what changes after that is told again.

acked_all.one: Noted — one entry is normal now.

state.open_title: Not noted yet: it counts at the team lead, on his picture and on the Dashboard
state.noted_title: You know about it: this state is normal now
state.watch_title: He took over the watch here and noted what was normal then

noted.baseline: Closed on {when}, when he took over the watch anew.
noted.auto: Noted by himself on {when}: User Scripts starts a script «in the background» through atd — nothing to tell.

adopt.flash_extra: «I know, thanks»: the file as it is now is normal.

check.quiet: The night watchman's watch book has nothing open
check.quiet_how: Whatever he finds different from normal shows up here until you note it on his page.

check.posture.one: The night watchman has one security recommendation
check.posture.other: The night watchman has {n} security recommendations

check.posture_how: On his page under «How secure does it stand?» — each with why and where in Unraid. Advice, not something to do.

check.login_new_ip.one: Login from a new address: {user} from {ip} ({service})
check.login_new_ip.other: {n} logins from new addresses, the newest: {user} from {ip} ({service})

check.login_new_ip_how: If that was you (a new device, a VPN), «I know, thanks» on the night watchman's page adds the address to the known ones. If not: change root's password and check who can reach the server from outside (Settings → Management Access, port forwardings on your router).

check.login_failures.other: Failed logins from {n} addresses, the newest: {ip} ({service})

check.login_failures_how: Someone tried to log in and failed again and again. A device of yours with an old password? Correct it there. An address from outside: the server can be reached from the internet — close the port forwarding or put a VPN in front. Unraid locks the WebGUI login of an address for 15 minutes after three failures.

check.container_new.other: {n} new containers with special rights, the newest: {name} ({rights})

check.container_new_how: A container with such rights reaches deep into the server. Installed on purpose: note it on the night watchman's page. If not: look at it under Docker and remove it.

check.container_privileged.other: {n} containers now run privileged, the newest: {name}

check.container_privileged_how: A privileged container can do nearly anything on the server. Switched on yourself (Docker → the container → Edit → Privileged): note it. If not: switch it off again.

check.container_host.other: {n} containers now use the host directly, the newest: {name} ({rights})

check.container_host_how: With the host's network or processes a container sees the server itself. Intended: note it. If not: set its network type back under Docker → the container → Edit.

check.container_ports.other: {n} containers publish new ports, the newest: {name} ({rights})

check.container_ports_how: New ports make the app reachable in your network — and from outside through a port forwarding. Intended: note it.

check.container_rights.other: {n} containers have new rights, the newest: {name} ({rights})

check.container_rights_how: Capabilities, devices or the Docker socket give a container more power over the server. Intended: note it. If not: remove them under Docker → the container → Edit.
check.plugin_new_how: A plugin runs as root on the server. Installed it yourself: note it on the night watchman's page. If not: remove it under Plugins.

check.plugin_source.other: {n} plugins update from somewhere else now, the newest: {name} from {source}

check.plugin_source_how: The plugin takes its updates from another place now — usually the author moved. Check that it is still the same project, then note it.
check.flash_go_how: /boot/config/go runs as root at every start of the server. Changed it yourself: note it. If not: look at it in a terminal (the night watchman never reads its text).

check.flash_extra.one: A file in /boot/extra is new or changed: {file}
check.flash_extra.other: {n} files in /boot/extra are new or changed, the newest: {file}

check.flash_extra_how: Packages in /boot/extra are installed at every start of the server. Put there by you: note it. If not: remove it.

check.flash_user.other: {n} new users on the flash, the newest: {user}

check.flash_user_how: Users are added under Users. Added yourself: note it. If not: remove the user.
check.flash_password_how: Changed it yourself (Users): note it. If not: set a new password for this user right away.

check.flash_ssh_key.other: {n} new SSH keys, the newest for {user}: {key}

check.flash_ssh_key_how: A key lets its owner log in by SSH without a password. Yours: note it. If not: remove it under Users → the user → SSH authorized keys.

check.share_public.one: {share} is now open to guests over {proto}
check.share_public.other: {n} shares are now open to guests, the newest: {share} over {proto}

check.share_public_how: Guests reach it without a password. Intended: note it. If not: set the share's security to Private (Shares → the share → SMB Security Settings or NFS Security Settings).

notify.login_new_ip.other: Night watchman: {n} logins from new addresses

notify.login_failures.other: Night watchman: failed logins from {n} addresses

notify.container_new.other: Night watchman: {n} new containers with special rights

notify.container_host.other: Night watchman: {n} containers now use the host directly

notify.plugin_source.other: Night watchman: {n} plugins update from elsewhere

notify.footer: The night watchman keeps all of it in his watch book in the office. «I know, thanks» there makes it the new normal. A switch there turns these reports off.
watch.title: What I keep an eye on
watch.sub: What is normal: what he saw when he took over the watch, and what you noted since. What gets safer (fewer rights, a share closed) becomes normal by itself. Counted and listed is what is there now: what went (a container, a plugin, a share) leaves the list — he still remembers it a while, so one that comes back as it was is no news.
watch.none: He records it on his first round.

watch.fail_ips_sum.one: one address — its failures are only counted
watch.fail_ips_sum.other: {n} addresses — their failures are only counted

watch.containers_wait: Docker wasn't running when he took over — he learns the containers on the next round Docker answers.

watch.go_lines.one: one line — he keeps only a fingerprint of it
watch.go_lines.other: {n} lines — he keeps only fingerprints of them

watch.shares_none: none — every share needs a login
watch.shares_wait: Unraid's list of shares wasn't there when he took over — he learns it on the next round.
help.book_text: Every entry is something that was different from normal: when, what, from where. A row unfolds to its details. «new» counts at the team lead, on his picture and on Unraid's Dashboard until you note it; the book keeps the last {keep} entries, noted ones for {days} days.
help.ack_text: Makes the state the entry names the new normal — the address joins the known ones, the container keeps its rights, the plugin its source. Then only what changes after it is told again. «I know, thanks» on his finding at the team lead counts here too.
help.normal_text: On his first round after hiring he records what is there and reports nothing for it — also the login addresses in the syslog. Hired again later, he takes a fresh look.
help.round_text: Every five minutes in the background, also with the office closed. «A round now» doesn't wait.
help.logins_text: WebGUI and SSH logins from the syslog: a login from an address he hasn't seen yet; {burst} or more failed logins from one address within {minutes} minutes. He keeps the names tried only when they are users of this server — somebody may have typed a password into the name field.
help.containers_text: Newly privileged, the host's network or processes, new ports, capabilities, devices, the Docker socket or the whole server mounted — shown as the flags of docker run. A new container only counts when it has such rights.
help.plugins_text: A new plugin, or one that takes its updates from another place now (the host; on GitHub and the like also the owner).
help.flash_text: /boot/config/go, files in /boot/extra, users, changed passwords and SSH keys. Of go he keeps fingerprints of the lines, of passwords only a fingerprint of each — never the text.
help.shares_text: A share (also a disk, a pool or the flash) that guests now reach without a password, over SMB or NFS — as Unraid applies it.
help.notify_text: Important kinds go to Unraid's notifications right away (the bell, mail or push): per kind one message an hour at most, so a burst gives one. New ports and capabilities only go into the book. The switch at «The last round» turns the reports off; what comes meanwhile is never told later.
help.safe_text: He changes nothing on the server and reads only what lives in RAM or on the flash — no disk wakes up. Not Fix Common Problems' checks (a root password, plugins Community Applications doesn't know, the FTP server once it has users): his tips are what it doesn't look at, his watch book only what changed.
group_title.sched: What starts on its own as root: crontabs, the plugins' schedules, User Scripts, at jobs, notification agents
entry.cron_twice: Runs twice — in root's own crontab and in Unraid's ({lines}): {jobs}
entry.cron_office: The office's own schedule is in root's own crontab too ({lines}): {jobs}
entry.at_job: A job in atd's queue, due {when}: {cmd}
adopt.cron_new: «I know, thanks»: these lines are normal.
adopt.cron_twice: «I know, thanks»: these doubled lines are normal — they still run twice until they are removed. Only new doubles are told again.
adopt.cron_office: «I know, thanks»: these lines are normal — they still run until they are removed.
adopt.cron_file: «I know, thanks»: the schedule as it is now is normal.
adopt.cron_file_foreign: «I know, thanks»: the file as it is now is normal.
adopt.script_new: «I know, thanks»: the script and its schedule are normal.
adopt.script_changed: «I know, thanks»: the script and its schedule as they are now are normal.
adopt.at_job: «I know, thanks»: this job is normal.
adopt.notify_agent: «I know, thanks»: the agent as it is now is normal.
check.cron_new_how: Lines in root's own crontab (crontab -l) — or another user's, or a file in /etc/cron.d — run as root until the next reboot. VM Backup writes its schedule there, a few older plugins too. The watch book has the file's time and what the syslog said then. Yours or a plugin's you set up: note it. If not: look at crontab -l in Unraid's terminal and find out who wrote it.
check.cron_twice_how: These lines are in root's own crontab (crontab -l) and in Unraid's (/etc/cron.d/root, built from the plugins' schedules). Unraid's cron reads both, so each of them starts twice: user scripts, checks, backups. Usually a plugin that writes root's own crontab (crontab -l | … | crontab -) took a copy along — the watch book has the file's time and what the syslog said then. The office changes nothing there. To keep a copy on the flash and remove only the doubled lines, in Unraid's terminal: {fix}
check.cron_office: The office's own schedule is in root's own crontab too ({lines}): {jobs}
check.cron_office_how: The office keeps its schedules (the backup, snapshots, Jack Emby's runs, the look at the agent) only in its own cron file on the flash. A copy in root's own crontab runs as well — an old copy at another time starts a second backup. Usually a plugin that writes root's own crontab took it along; the watch book has the file's time and what the syslog said then. The office changes nothing there. To keep a copy on the flash and remove these lines, in Unraid's terminal: {fix}
check.cron_file_how: The plugins' .cron files on the flash are what Unraid's crontab is built from — they survive a reboot. A plugin writes them when you set its schedule (the office too, for its own). Set by you: note it. If not: look at the file.

check.cron_file_foreign.one: A schedule of no installed plugin: {file}
check.cron_file_foreign.other: {n} schedules of no installed plugin, the newest: {file}

check.cron_file_foreign_how: A .cron file on the flash in the folder of a plugin that isn't installed. Unraid leaves it out for now — but it runs as soon as a plugin of that name is installed, and it survives every reboot. A leftover you know: note it, or delete the file. If you don't know it: look at it first.
check.script_new_how: User scripts run as root — on their schedule, or when the array starts or stops. Added by you: note it. If not: look at it under Settings → User Scripts.
check.script_changed_how: Its content or its schedule is different now. Changed by you: note it. If not: look at it under Settings → User Scripts.

check.at_job.one: A job waiting in atd's queue: {cmd}
check.at_job.other: {n} jobs waiting in atd's queue, the newest: {cmd}

check.at_job_how: atd runs it once at its time, as root. The office's own jobs (backups, restores, installs) are left out — this one isn't the office's. Started by you or a plugin: note it. If not: in Unraid's terminal atq lists the queue, at -c <number> shows a job, atrm <number> removes it.

check.notify_agent.other: {n} notification agents new or changed, the newest: {name}

check.notify_agent_how: Every file in Unraid's agents folder runs as root with each notification (Settings → Notifications → Notification Agents). Set up or changed by you: note it. If not: look at it there and switch it off.
notify.cron_office: Night watchman: the office's schedule in root's own crontab

notify.cron_file_foreign.one: Night watchman: a schedule of no installed plugin
notify.cron_file_foreign.other: Night watchman: {n} schedules of no installed plugin

notify.at_job.one: Night watchman: a job in atd's queue
notify.at_job.other: Night watchman: {n} jobs in atd's queue

entry.at_userscript: User Script {name} started in the background (through atd)
adopt.at_userscript: Nothing to do: User Scripts runs scripts «in the background» through atd.

check.at_userscript.one: User Script {name} started in the background
check.at_userscript.other: {n} User Scripts started in the background, the newest: {name}

check.at_userscript_how: Nothing to do — the User Scripts plugin starts «Run in background» through atd. He notes these himself.

notify.at_userscript.one: Night watchman: a User Script started in the background
notify.at_userscript.other: Night watchman: {n} User Scripts started in the background

detail.evidence_none: Nothing about plugins, scripts or cron in the syslog two minutes before or after.
detail.fix_note: For Unraid's terminal — the office never runs it.
detail.office_cron: The office's own cron file — it changes when you set a schedule in the office.
watch.sched_wait: He learns it on his next round.

watch.crontab_twice.one: one line in both crontabs — noted

watch.at_sum.one: one job not of the office — noted
watch.at_sum.other: {n} jobs not of the office — noted

help.sched_text: What starts on its own as root — where an intruder settles in, and where a plugin can quietly double jobs. Root's own crontab (crontab -l) next to Unraid's (/etc/cron.d/root): new lines, lines in both (they run twice), the office's own lines there (they belong in its cron file only — an old copy starts a second backup) — each with the file's time and what the syslog said around it. Also other users' crontabs and /etc/cron.d's other files, the plugins' .cron files on the flash (they survive a reboot), User Scripts and their schedules, jobs in atd's queue that aren't the office's, and Unraid's notification agents (of those only a fingerprint: they hold tokens). He changes nothing; where something can be undone, the entry has the command for Unraid's terminal. A User Script started «in the background» goes through atd too: when the job is exactly that, it is a plain line in the book, noted by itself. Lines whose program went with its plugin are leftovers, not a danger: Ms. Whereabouts tells those.
fact.quiet: Nothing open in the watch book
group_title.flow: Who pulls how much: clients over SMB, NFS, SSH and the WebGUI, containers, what is written into ZFS shares, SMB's users and machines
entry.smb_hour: SMB session from {ip} ({user}) at an hour it never used: {hours}
flow.usual: usually at most {size} per hour at this time
flow.learning: more than {size} in one round while I'm still learning what is normal
flow.learning_share: {pct} % of the share while I'm still learning what is normal
gone.kept: {size} of it still in its snapshots.
gone.who_clients: Moving data over SMB, NFS or SSH then: {list}.
gone.who_server: No client moved data over SMB, NFS or SSH then — it came from the server itself.
gone.disk: Measured for the whole disk ({fs}), not per share.
adopt.flow_client: «I know, thanks»: that much is normal for this client from now on — only far more is told again.
adopt.flow_container: «I know, thanks»: that much is normal for this container from now on — only far more is told again.
adopt.flow_written: «I know, thanks»: that much writing is normal for this share from now on — only far more is told again.
adopt.flow_gone: «I know, thanks»: that much going is normal for this share from now on — only far more is told again.
adopt.smb_user: «I know, thanks»: the user is normal on SMB.
adopt.smb_client: «I know, thanks»: the machine is normal on SMB — from then on I learn its hours.
adopt.smb_hour: «I know, thanks»: these hours are normal for this machine.

check.flow_client.other: {n} times more pulled than usual, the newest: {ip} — {size} over {service}

check.flow_client_how: A client fetched far more from the server than it usually does at this time of the week. A backup, a sync or a copy you know of: note it on the night watchman's page — that much is normal for it then. If not: find out which device has that address (your router lists them) and check which shares it can reach (Shares → the share → SMB Security Settings). Which files were read can't be told — that would need Samba's audit logging.

check.flow_container.other: {n} times containers sent more than usual, the newest: {name} — {size}

check.flow_container_how: A container sent far more over the network than it usually does at this time of the week — to clients, other containers or the internet. An upload, a sync or a backup you know of: note it. If not: look at its logs (Docker → the container → Logs) and at what it can reach.

check.flow_written.other: {n} times much written into shares, the newest: {share} — {size}

check.flow_written_how: Far more was written into this share than usual — rewritten files count too. A big copy, a move or an app's update you know of: note it. If not, and files suddenly have odd names or don't open, that is the pattern of ransomware: disconnect the clients that write there (smbstatus in Unraid's terminal shows who is connected) and keep the snapshots — they hold the files as they were.

check.flow_gone.other: {n} times much gone from shares, the newest: {share} — {size}

check.flow_gone_how: Far more vanished from this share than usual — deleted, or moved somewhere he doesn't look. A cleanup or a move you know of: note it. If not: the entry says who moved data over SMB, NFS or SSH then — or that it came from the server itself (a shell, a container, a job). Keep the share's snapshots, they still hold what was deleted (Ms. Snapshotini can hold them); smbstatus in Unraid's terminal shows who is connected.

check.smb_user.other: {n} new users on SMB, the newest: {user} (from {ip})

check.smb_user_how: A user who never connected over SMB before did now. Yours: note it. If not: check the users under Users and the shares' SMB security.

check.smb_client.other: {n} new machines on SMB, the newest: {ip} ({user})

check.smb_client_how: A machine that never connected over SMB before did now. A new device of yours, or an address handed out anew by your router: note it.

check.smb_hour.one: SMB session at an unusual hour: {ip} ({user}, {hours})
check.smb_hour.other: {n} machines started SMB sessions at unusual hours, the newest: {ip} ({user}, {hours})

check.smb_hour_how: This machine started a session at an hour of the week it never used before. Up late, or a scheduled job: note it.

notify.flow_container.other: Night watchman: {n} containers sent more than usual

notify.flow_gone.other: Night watchman: much gone from {n} shares

help.flow_text: Who pulls how much — from what the server counts anyway, every five minutes. Per client and service (SMB, NFS, SSH with SFTP and rsync, the WebGUI with its File Manager): what the server sent over the connections open at the round; a connection that opened and closed between two rounds is lost. Per container: what it sent — to clients, other containers and the internet; containers on the host's network can't be told apart from the server. Per ZFS share: what was written since its latest snapshot — rewritten files count, the pattern of ransomware; without snapshots only growth shows, shares on XFS or btrfs disks can't be measured, sleeping pools are left alone. He learns hour by hour for {keep} days: unusual is far more ({factor} ×) than at that time of the week, and at least {min} in the hour. During the first {learn} days only clear cases: more than {new} in one round, or {part} % of a share. «I know, thanks» raises that one's normal. The office's own work is expected: Kopia's upload and what the backup writes into its backup place, all that a restore writes back; its snapshots are no writing. Media servers streaming are expected too. SMB: a new user, a new machine, a session started at an hour that machine never used.
help.flow_gone_text: What vanished from a share between two rounds — deleted, or moved somewhere else; as untypical as mass writing. On ZFS per share and exactly: how much less its datasets hold (pools asleep are named, never woken) and how much of it its snapshots still keep. On XFS and btrfs disks only per disk, from their used space — a disk holds several shares, the entry names those with a folder there; files a btrfs snapshot still holds free no space until the snapshot goes, and rounds right after its snapshots changed are left out. Learned like the writing; during the first {learn} days told only when one round takes {new} or {part} % of a share. Each entry says who moved data over SMB, NFS or SSH at that moment — or that nobody did and it came from the server itself. Not a loss: the office's own work, the mover, EmbyCache, the gather, rsync --remove-source-files, Ms. Dustdevil's storeroom (putting away and emptying), snapshots pruned.
help.flow_not_text: Which files were read: that needs Samba's audit logging (full_audit), far too much for Unraid's 128 MB /var/log — he doesn't switch it on. Where data goes on the internet: that needs the kernel's connection accounting (sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_acct=1, off on Unraid) — an option for experts; he never switches it on. What clients upload only shows as written into ZFS shares.
help.posture_text: How the server stands now, not what changed — looked at on every round: shares open to everyone (also a disk, a pool or the flash), Telnet, Unraid's FTP server, the CPU's protection against Spectre-like flaws (and VMScape with VMs), privileged containers. Each with why and a link into Unraid. «I know, thanks» is kept on the server for every browser; the tip comes back when what it is about changes. The team lead only hears how many there are, as good to know.
help.grafana_text: Where the consultant found Grafana with the office's dashboard, the data flow's groups link their history there (what the server sent per service, what was written into shares) — a link to the panel, opening in a new tab; nothing is embedded.
